title: Barclays Bank plc v. O’Brien
lead: A wife signed security for her husband’s business after he misstated its extent, and the bank’s failure to give its planned explanation left it with constructive notice of her right to resist enforcement.

actors.name: Nicholas and Bridget Mary O’Brien
actors.role: Joint homeowners; husband guarantor and wife surety

actors.name: Heathrow Fabrications Ltd.
actors.role: Company in which Nicholas alone had a financial interest

proceedings: Trial judge ordered possession despite finding the husband’s misrepresentation.
Court of Appeal limited enforcement against Bridget to the £60,000 she understood.
House of Lords dismissed Barclays’ appeal and affirmed that order with costs.
limits: Undue influence had failed below and was not pursued in the House; misrepresentation was the operative wrong. The House rejected a special married-women equity and applied notice principles. Historical safeguards are not a later-law certification.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A business overdraft expands against the family home
sections.cue: The wife has no direct company interest
paragraphs: Nicholas and Bridget Mary O’Brien jointly owned their Slough home subject to about £25,000 owed to a building society. Nicholas, a chartered accountant, had an interest in Heathrow Fabrications; Bridget had none. Early in 1987 its Barclays overdraft repeatedly exceeded £40,000, with dishonoured cheques. A temporary £60,000 limit did not solve matters, and June 15 debt reached £98,000.

On June 22 Nicholas and the Woolwich manager agreed to a £135,000 facility, falling to £120,000 after three weeks. Nicholas would give an unlimited guarantee, secured through both spouses’ charge over their home. He falsely told Bridget it secured only £60,000 and would be released shortly when the home was remortgaged.

sources.pinpoint: Browne-Wilkinson, The facts, lines105–110,124–127; Decision, line250

sections.title: The bank’s planned warnings are never delivered
paragraphs: The Woolwich manager sent the papers to Burnham with instructions to explain current facilities of £107,000, the projected £135,000, the documents, and solicitor consultation if uncertain. Those instructions were not followed. Nicholas signed July 1; Bridget attended with him July 2 and signed the charge and side letter before a clerk. The letter acknowledged a guarantee copy, security, and an independent-advice recommendation and referred to July 3 documents, but she received neither explanation nor advice recommendation or guarantee copy and did not read them.

By October company debt exceeded £154,000. Barclays demanded under the guarantee in November and sued for possession after nonpayment. The trial judge found Nicholas’s misrepresentation but ordered possession because he considered the bank not responsible. Undue influence was rejected and not pursued in the House.

The Court of Appeal reversed, leaving the charge unenforceable against Bridget except for the £60,000 she thought she secured. Scott L.J. discussed both agency and a special equity for vulnerable sureties in influential relationships. Barclays appealed.

sources.pinpoint: The facts, lines109–127; Court of Appeal, lines128–133

sections.title: The House uses ordinary notice principles
sections.cue: Marriage alone does not prove undue influence
paragraphs: Lord Browne-Wilkinson separated wrongdoing from its effect on the lender. A surety first needed a legal or equitable basis against the principal debtor, such as misrepresentation or undue influence. Simple misunderstanding did not confer a general right to repudiate. The equity then bound the creditor through agency or actual or constructive notice. Agency seldom fit a debtor obtaining assistance for his own financing; notice supplied the ordinary connection.

A transaction facially offering the wife no financial advantage, with substantial risk of spousal wrongdoing in transactions of that type, put the bank on inquiry without proof it knew an actual lie. Known trust, emotional involvement, and financial reliance could create vulnerability, but marriage did not automatically presume undue influence. The court distinguished actual influence from presumptions arising in recognized confidential categories or relationships proved on the facts.

Reconsidering Turnbull v. Duval exposed uncertain wrongdoing, an agent’s fiduciary role, and artificial later agency theories. The House rejected a special equity for married women or sureties that demanded proof of understanding beyond ordinary principles. It sought protection without making jointly owned homes unavailable for business finance. Comparable known cohabitation or financial trust, including elderly parents misled by a son, could trigger the same principles.

sources.pinpoint: Policy and undue-influence sections, lines134–168; Turnbull and conclusions, lines169–247

sections.title: Reasonable precautions would have exposed this misinformation
paragraphs: Ordinarily the lender could meet its responsibility through a private meeting without the husband, explanation of potential liability, a risk warning, and encouragement of independent advice. Exceptional knowledge making undue influence probable could require insisting on separate advice. Past precautions depended on circumstances. Written warnings alone could go unread or be intercepted; banking recommendations and the 1992 code already contemplated advice and warnings, making private discussion the principal added burden.

Barclays knew the marriage and that Bridget was securing a company in which only Nicholas had a financial stake. It therefore was on inquiry. Explanation of the actual facilities and increase would contradict the supposed £60,000 short-lived exposure. Instead it merely witnessed signature, giving it constructive notice of the misrepresentation and her resulting equity.

On October 21, 1993, Lords Templeman, Lowry, Slynn, and Woolf agreed with Browne-Wilkinson. The House unanimously dismissed the appeal and affirmed the Court of Appeal’s order, with respondents’ appeal costs against Barclays. It did not find undue influence, award damages against Nicholas, or make every misunderstood guarantee unenforceable.

sources.pinpoint: Conclusions (a), lines217–238; Decision, lines249–260; parliamentary order, lines41–101
